Issued at 405 AM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026

A negatively-tilted upper level ridge extends from Alberta/ 
Saskatchewan to Georgia/Florida early this morning. The ridge 
axis cuts through the Dakotas over a veering low level wind 
profile. Low level warm air and moisture advection will persist 
through the day today as underlying surface flow remains 
easterly between a surface ridge axis extending northwest from 
the Great Lakes and a lee cyclone over Wyoming. Low stratus is 
forecast to expand northward across the state this morning and 
afternoon, and the depth of the near-surface saturated layer may
be sufficient for areas of mist or drizzle. Isolated to 
scattered showers could also develop over central and eastern 
North Dakota today ahead of 700 mb DCVA, but subsidence aloft 
could be a deterrent. Because of the extensive cloud cover, the 
high temperature forecast for today was lowered closer to the 
25th percentile of the NBM distribution, which gives upper 40s 
north central to mid 50s south.

Most of the state will remain under a deeper low level layer of
saturation tonight into Sunday, which may continue to promote 
areas of mist and drizzle. Models that simulate visibility would
indicate widespread dense fog tonight into Sunday, but this 
seems more like a low stratus episode where ceilings could lower
to the surface along areas of higher terrain. Low to medium 
chances for light rain also remain in the forecast tonight into 
Sunday, becoming more focused over northwest North Dakota as a 
mid level shortwave drifts through the area. Temperatures will 
remain mild overnight, with near-record warm lows mostly in the 
mid 40s to lower 50s. Sunday should be slightly warmer than 
today, but still closer to the NBM 25th percentile highs of 
lower 50s northwest to lower 60s south central and southeast 
given an overcast sky prevailing for most areas. 

A deep upper level trough will begin crossing the Rockies 
Sunday night, inducing lee cyclogenesis over Colorado. 
Meanwhile, a northern stream wave is projected to dig into the 
southern Canadian prairie provinces Monday morning and interact 
with the Colorado low and its parent upper trough. This sets 
the stage for a widespread rain event that will impact most, 
but perhaps not all of North Dakota. The highest chances for 
rain (90 to 100 percent) enter southwest North Dakota late 
Sunday night and migrate eastward through the day Monday, 
departing to the east Monday night. Lower chances for lighter 
rain (20 to 40 percent) remain in the forecast for central and 
eastern North Dakota through Tuesday, with higher- membership 
ensemble clusters favoring a slower departure of rain. Ensemble
mean QPF and threshold probabilities are lowest over north 
central North Dakota and increase in all southward facing 
directions. The highest amounts/chances by far are in southeast
North Dakota, but there is a secondary local maximum from 
southeast Montana into southwest North Dakota. NBM calibrated 
QPF output remains higher than that of raw global ensembles, 
especially at higher thresholds. But even global ensembles are 
now showing medium chances for exceeding 2 inches of rain in 
the southern James River Valley. In addition, the ECMWF EFI and 
shift-of-tails products do support an anomalously high QPF 
event, so the NBM calibrated QPF may not be overly aggressive. 
Temperatures will remain above freezing through the duration of
the precipitation event. Sunday night lows are forecast to 
remain in the 40s, followed by mid 40s to mid 50s for highs on 
Monday. Monday night will be colder than Sunday night, but 
forecast low temperatures below freezing are only anticipated 
if and/or where precipitation ends. Lastly, the passage of the 
surface low to the south and east will likely bring a period of 
strong northeast to northwest winds across southern North 
Dakota Monday through Monday night, with medium chances of 
winds reaching advisory criteria. 

Ensemble consensus broadly supports upper level ridging over 
the central CONUS for the middle of next week, but 
deterministic guidance implies the ridge could be interrupted 
by lower-amplitude shortwaves that are being washed out in mean
height fields due to timing and location uncertainty. 
Significant ensemble spread in the synoptic pattern emerges by 
the end of next week, but the jet stream is favored to remain 
south of the Northern Plains. The NBM maintains near to above 
normal temperatures and a dry forecast from mid to late next 
week.
